title: Prosecutor v. Johan Tarčulovski — police operation in Ljuboten
holding: In its Trial Judgment of 10 July 2008, the ICTY Trial Chamber found Johan Tarčulovski guilty under Article 7(1) of ordering, planning and instigating the murder of three residents, wanton destruction of houses or other property belonging to twelve residents, and cruel treatment of thirteen residents at Adem Ametovski’s house and ten residents at Braca’s house. He received a single sentence of 12 years’ imprisonment. The two accused were treated differently: Tarčulovski was found guilty on the three counts, while Ljube Boškoski was found not guilty on all counts.
key_reasoning: Tarčulovski coordinated the logistical preparations and police and army support, personally led the police operation, and exercised effective leadership and control over the police in the village.
The Chamber found that the actions of the police in the village were at Tarčulovski’s direction.
The Chamber concluded that Tarčulovski was criminally responsible for ordering, planning and instigating the offences committed in the village by police.
The Chamber found that an internal armed conflict existed in Macedonia by August 2001.
The Chamber found that the pattern of conduct in the village was a deliberate and indiscriminate attack on residents of Albanian ethnicity, and that it was not a law enforcement operation.
The Chamber found that he did not participate in a joint criminal enterprise, and that his direct role was in ordering, planning and instigating the offences, not merely aiding and abetting.
facts: Whether an internal armed conflict existed in Macedonia at the time was highly contested at trial. The Defence submitted that the events in Ljuboten were part of a law-enforcement operation to search for members of the National Liberation Army (NLA) and prevent future attacks; the Prosecution disputed that account and argued that Ljuboten was neither an NLA stronghold nor a logistics base. The parties presented conflicting evidence about events in the village. On 10 August 2001, a land mine attack at a location close to Ljuboten killed eight soldiers and wounded others. On the morning of 12 August 2001, at least 60 to 70 and possibly more than 100 reserve police, including members of a private security agency called Kometa, entered Ljuboten with incendiary material and an armoured personnel carrier. It was alleged that Johan Tarčulovski, a relatively junior police officer, commanded the police who entered the village and was present when the crimes were committed. Macedonian army units positioned in the surrounding mountains provided mortar and other fire support. At one house, police fired many shots into the house and through its open front door; an unarmed man in civilian clothing was shot and later died there. A car and construction materials in the yard were set on fire. Police then set fire to a nearby house and about ten more houses along the village’s main road. Thirteen men, with women also present, were found sheltering in basements at the family compound of Adem Ametovski. The men were unarmed, wore civilian clothes, and did not resist. Valuables and identification papers were taken from them, and the men were forced to lie on the ground and to pull their clothing over their eyes and heads. Police beat and kicked them, threatened them with knives, and one man was shot in the arm or hand. One man was shot and died while the others were on the ground. Most of the remaining men were escorted to Braca’s house at the village entrance; two elderly men remained at the compound, where one was shot and died. The ten men taken to Braca’s house were further beaten, and some lost consciousness. They were later detained at Mirkovci police station, where they were beaten by other police; one died in hospital the next day. At the outskirts of the village, five men ran from a house as police approached, and came under fire from police and army positions; two escaped and three bodies were found. There was evidence of firearms near the bodies, but the same weapons had also been attributed to some of the men earlier found at Adem Ametovski’s compound. It could not be determined whether the three men died from police or army fire, and the evidence also allowed for the possibility that they had fired at police or army. In the afternoon, men fleeing Ljuboten were separated from women and subjected to cruel treatment at a checkpoint manned by different police, and many were further mistreated at police stations in Skopje. Tarčulovski was himself acting under orders in carrying out the police operation.

question: Was a police officer alleged to have led an operation in a village criminally responsible for killings, cruel treatment, and destruction of villagers' homes committed by police during that operation?
